questions.prompt: Two unrelated processes need to exchange a large volume of data repeatedly on one machine. Which IPC method often has the lowest per-message copying overhead after setup?
options: shared memory
ordinary signal delivery
a process exit status
a named semaphore alone
answer: shared memory
questions.explanation: Shared memory lets both processes access a common mapped region, avoiding repeated kernel-mediated copying of the payload. Synchronization is still required.

questions.prompt: Processes use shared memory for a producer-consumer buffer. What additional mechanism is needed to coordinate safe access?
options: Synchronization such as semaphores or mutexes
A separate copy of the buffer per process
A new PID for each item
A CPU scheduling priority only
answer: Synchronization such as semaphores or mutexes
questions.explanation: Shared memory provides common bytes but does not serialize conflicting accesses. Locks, semaphores, or another protocol must coordinate producers and consumers.

questions.prompt: An anonymous pipe is created before fork. Which processes can typically access it?
options: The parent and its descendants that inherit its descriptors
Any process on the network
Only unrelated processes that know its name
Only the kernel
answer: The parent and its descendants that inherit its descriptors
questions.explanation: An anonymous pipe is accessed through file descriptors. Forked descendants inherit descriptor references, whereas unrelated processes typically need another mechanism.

questions.prompt: A pipe has no data, but its write end remains open. What does a blocking read normally do?
options: Wait until data arrives or all writers close
Return end-of-file immediately
Write a zero byte
Terminate the reader
answer: Wait until data arrives or all writers close
questions.explanation: An empty pipe is not at EOF while a writer remains open. A blocking read waits for data; EOF is reported only after all write ends close.

questions.prompt: A pipe is empty and every write descriptor referring to it is closed. What does a read return?
options: End-of-file
It blocks forever
A fabricated zero byte
An error indicating the reader is a zombie
answer: End-of-file
questions.explanation: Once the buffer is empty and no writers remain, the reader observes EOF. The read does not wait for a writer that can no longer exist.

questions.prompt: A process writes to a pipe after all read descriptors have closed. What is the usual consequence?
options: A broken-pipe error or signal
The data is stored indefinitely
A new reader is created
The write succeeds and creates a FIFO
answer: A broken-pipe error or signal
questions.explanation: With no readers, the write cannot be delivered; Unix-like systems typically report EPIPE and may send SIGPIPE.

questions.prompt: A parent intends to send data to its child through a pipe. Which end should the parent close after setting up the child?s descriptors if it will only write?
options: The read end
The write end
Both ends
Neither end under any circumstance
answer: The read end
questions.explanation: Closing unused ends is essential: the parent keeps the write end, while closing its read end prevents accidental reads and helps EOF detection in the child.

questions.prompt: A pipe has capacity 64 KiB and currently contains 60 KiB. A writer attempts a blocking write of 8 KiB. What is generally possible?
options: The write may block until enough space becomes available
The entire write must always succeed immediately
The pipe discards its oldest 4 KiB
The reader is terminated
answer: The write may block until enough space becomes available
questions.explanation: Only 4 KiB of space remains. A blocking writer may wait for a reader to consume data; atomicity and partial-write behavior depend on size and API guarantees.

questions.prompt: Two processes need a persistent named byte stream accessible through the filesystem namespace. Which mechanism fits?
options: FIFO (named pipe)
anonymous pipe only
exit status
shared stack
answer: FIFO (named pipe)
questions.explanation: A FIFO has a filesystem name and can connect processes that did not inherit a common anonymous pipe descriptor. It provides stream semantics.

questions.prompt: A message queue stores two messages of different lengths. Which property distinguishes it from a byte-stream pipe?
options: Message boundaries can be preserved
It can only transmit one byte
It requires the sender and receiver to run simultaneously
It is always shared memory
answer: Message boundaries can be preserved
questions.explanation: Message queues retain discrete messages, while a pipe exposes an ordered byte stream without inherent message boundaries.

questions.prompt: A receiver requests messages of type 5 from a message queue containing types 2, 5, and 8. What can the queue provide?
options: A message matching the requested type
Only the oldest message regardless of type
A direct pointer into the sender?s stack
A copy of the receiver process
answer: A message matching the requested type
questions.explanation: Typed selection is a common message-queue feature, allowing a receiver to retrieve a chosen class of message rather than strictly the oldest.

questions.prompt: A process sends a signal to another process. Which is the most accurate description?
options: A limited asynchronous notification, generally not a bulk-data channel
A reliable arbitrary-length message stream
A shared memory mapping
A process creation operation
answer: A limited asynchronous notification, generally not a bulk-data channel
questions.explanation: Signals notify a process of events and carry limited information. They are generally unsuitable for transferring large structured payloads.

questions.prompt: A shared-memory segment is mapped at different virtual addresses in two processes. Can both processes still access the same underlying bytes?
options: Yes, virtual addresses can differ while mappings refer to the same shared pages
No, shared memory requires identical virtual addresses
Only if the processes have the same PID
Only after one process exits
answer: Yes, virtual addresses can differ while mappings refer to the same shared pages
questions.explanation: Shared mappings can map the same physical pages at distinct virtual addresses. Processes use their own pointers to access the common storage.

questions.prompt: A process stores a raw pointer in shared memory for another process to use. Why can this be unsafe?
options: The pointer may not be valid at the other process?s mapping address
Pointers are prohibited in shared memory
The shared pages become read-only
The other process receives a different physical disk
answer: The pointer may not be valid at the other process?s mapping address
questions.explanation: A virtual pointer is meaningful in one process?s address space. If the segment is mapped elsewhere in another process, the stored address may refer to unrelated memory.

questions.prompt: Which IPC endpoint is commonly used for communication between processes on different machines?
options: socket
anonymous pipe
process exit status
local mutex only
answer: socket
questions.explanation: Sockets provide communication endpoints that can use local or network protocols. Anonymous pipes and ordinary exit statuses are not general network channels.

questions.prompt: A TCP socket provides a byte stream. What must an application do to distinguish two logical messages sent consecutively?
options: Define framing, such as length prefixes or delimiters
Assume each send maps to one receive
Use a new process for every byte
Rely on TCP packet boundaries
answer: Define framing, such as length prefixes or delimiters
questions.explanation: TCP preserves byte order but not application message boundaries. The application needs an explicit framing protocol to split the stream.

questions.prompt: A datagram socket transmits two datagrams of lengths 20 and 40 bytes. Which property is generally preserved at the receiving interface?
options: The datagrams remain separate messages
They are concatenated into an unmarked byte stream
Their order is always guaranteed by every datagram protocol
They share one process stack
answer: The datagrams remain separate messages
questions.explanation: Datagram APIs preserve message boundaries, unlike byte streams. Delivery and ordering depend on the protocol; UDP does not guarantee either.

questions.prompt: A process pair communicates using shared memory. Which statement about data transfer is correct?
options: Both processes can read and write the same mapped region
The kernel copies every load and store between them
Only the creator can access the region
The shared region has no address in either process
answer: Both processes can read and write the same mapped region
questions.explanation: Each process maps the shared region into its address space and accesses it directly. The kernel establishes mappings but need not mediate each memory access.

questions.prompt: A producer and consumer share a ring buffer of capacity N. The producer increments a shared head index without synchronization while the consumer reads it. What is the principal issue?
options: A data race can corrupt the protocol state
The pipe becomes full
The consumer?s PID changes
The buffer automatically serializes operations
answer: A data race can corrupt the protocol state
questions.explanation: The head index is shared mutable state. Unsynchronized concurrent reads and writes can violate the ring-buffer invariants and lead to lost or inconsistent items.

questions.prompt: A message queue is full and the sender performs a blocking send. What happens?
options: The sender may block until queue capacity is available
The oldest message is always overwritten
The queue grows without bound by definition
The receiver is terminated
answer: The sender may block until queue capacity is available
questions.explanation: A bounded queue cannot accept more data when full. A blocking send waits for space; nonblocking APIs can instead report that the queue is full.

questions.prompt: A receiver blocks waiting on an empty message queue. A sender places a message in it. Which state transition is typical for the receiver?
options: blocked to ready
running to terminated
ready to blocked
new to zombie
answer: blocked to ready
questions.explanation: Arrival of a matching message satisfies the receiver?s wait condition and makes it ready. It still needs CPU dispatch to run.

questions.prompt: A process sends an integer through a pipe by writing its in-memory representation. What portability issue can arise if the receiver uses a different architecture?
options: Endianness and representation may differ
Pipes cannot carry integers
The process IDs must match
The pipe converts the integer to text automatically
answer: Endianness and representation may differ
questions.explanation: A pipe transmits bytes without interpreting them. Different byte order, integer width, or representation can produce a different value at the receiver.

questions.prompt: Two processes need a local request-response channel with bidirectional communication. Which is a common choice?
options: Unix-domain socket
one-way anonymous pipe only
exit code
condition variable alone
answer: Unix-domain socket
questions.explanation: A Unix-domain socket provides local bidirectional communication and supports request-response designs. A single ordinary pipe is unidirectional.

questions.prompt: A process has duplicated descriptors for both ends of a pipe but never closes its own write end. Its child reads until EOF. What can happen?
options: The child may never see EOF after draining data
The child immediately gets EOF
The pipe changes into a message queue
The parent becomes a zombie
answer: The child may never see EOF after draining data
questions.explanation: EOF requires every write reference to close. The parent?s lingering write descriptor keeps the pipe logically open even after the child drains it.

questions.prompt: A pipe write of size no larger than the platform?s PIPE_BUF is issued by each of two writers. What guarantee is commonly provided?
options: Each write is not interleaved with bytes from the other such write
The writes are always received in creation order
The pipe becomes bidirectional
Each reader gets a separate copy automatically
answer: Each write is not interleaved with bytes from the other such write
questions.explanation: POSIX atomicity for writes up to PIPE_BUF prevents interleaving of bytes from concurrent such writes. It does not generally guarantee which writer goes first.

questions.prompt: A pipe carries output from command A to command B. Which descriptor arrangement is needed for B to receive A?s output?
options: A?s write end connected to B?s read end
Both processes write to the same end
A?s read end connected to B?s write end
B?s standard input connected to its own write end
answer: A?s write end connected to B?s read end
questions.explanation: A pipeline connects the producer?s output descriptor to the pipe write end and the consumer?s input to the read end.

questions.prompt: A shared-memory producer writes a payload and then sets a ready flag without memory ordering. What may a consumer observe on a weakly ordered system?
options: The ready flag before the payload becomes visible
The producer?s PID instead of the flag
A guaranteed consistent payload order
Automatic locking by the MMU
answer: The ready flag before the payload becomes visible
questions.explanation: Without synchronization or ordering, stores may become visible in a different order. The consumer could observe readiness before all payload writes are visible.

questions.prompt: A program uses a semaphore to indicate that shared-memory data is ready. Which ordering is normally needed?
options: Write data before signaling; wait before reading
Signal before writing; read before waiting
No ordering, because shared memory is atomic
Close the shared-memory descriptor before each read
answer: Write data before signaling; wait before reading
questions.explanation: The producer must publish the payload before signaling. The consumer waits for the signal before reading, with the semaphore providing synchronization ordering.

questions.prompt: A process sends a signal while the receiver has that signal blocked. What is generally true?
options: The signal may remain pending until unblocked
The receiver must terminate immediately
The signal becomes a shared-memory message
The sender blocks until handled
answer: The signal may remain pending until unblocked
questions.explanation: A blocked signal is typically marked pending and delivered when unblocked, subject to signal semantics. Blocking it does not itself force termination.

questions.prompt: A socket server calls accept on a listening stream socket. What does accept typically return?
options: A new connected socket for one client
The server?s PID
The same listening socket after deletion
A shared-memory pointer
answer: A new connected socket for one client
questions.explanation: Accept creates or returns a separate connected endpoint for a client, while the listening socket remains available for further connection requests.

questions.prompt: A producer sends one 9000-byte message over a stream socket. The receiver reads 3000 bytes per call. How many reads are minimally needed to obtain all bytes if every read returns the requested amount?
questions.explanation: The byte stream contains 9000 bytes, and each read obtains 3000. Thus 9000 / 3000 = 3 reads are required.

questions.prompt: A sender writes 100 bytes to a TCP connection in one call. Is the receiver guaranteed to get exactly one 100-byte read?
options: No; TCP preserves bytes, not write-call boundaries
Yes, every write maps to one read
No; TCP may reorder the byte stream
Yes, if both processes use the same CPU
answer: No; TCP preserves bytes, not write-call boundaries
questions.explanation: TCP provides an ordered byte stream. The receiver may get the bytes in several reads or combine data from multiple writes.

questions.prompt: A UDP datagram of 1200 bytes is sent. The receiving application provides a buffer of only 800 bytes. What may happen?
options: The datagram may be truncated or discarded beyond the buffer
The remaining 400 bytes arrive as a second datagram
The sender automatically retries the remainder
The socket changes to TCP
answer: The datagram may be truncated or discarded beyond the buffer
questions.explanation: Datagram receive APIs deliver one message at a time; an undersized buffer can truncate the datagram (or report truncation), not split it into another datagram.

questions.prompt: A message queue receiver asks for a message but no matching type is present. What may a blocking receive do?
options: Wait until a matching message arrives
Return a fabricated message
Terminate the sender
Change all message types to the requested type
answer: Wait until a matching message arrives
questions.explanation: A blocking receive waits for an eligible message. If the API supports typed selection, other queued types may remain untouched.

questions.prompt: A shared-memory segment is mapped read-only in one process and read-write in another. Which statement is true?
options: The access permissions can differ by process mapping
The segment must become read-only everywhere
Neither process can write
The read-only mapping forces a copy at every read
answer: The access permissions can differ by process mapping
questions.explanation: Mapping protections are applied per address space. One process can be restricted to reads while another retains write access to the shared pages.

questions.prompt: A process unlinks a named shared-memory object while another process still has it mapped. What is generally true on Unix-like systems?
options: Existing mappings can remain usable until unmapped
All existing mappings vanish immediately
The other process is terminated
The object is converted into a FIFO
answer: Existing mappings can remain usable until unmapped
questions.explanation: Unlink removes the name, but active mappings or references can keep the underlying object alive until they are released.

questions.prompt: A named FIFO is opened for reading in blocking mode before any writer opens it. What commonly happens?
options: The open blocks until a writer opens the FIFO
It returns EOF immediately
It creates a writer process
It fails because FIFOs are unidirectional
answer: The open blocks until a writer opens the FIFO
questions.explanation: Blocking FIFO opens can wait for a corresponding endpoint. Exact details depend on flags, but the reader commonly blocks until a writer appears.

questions.prompt: A named FIFO is opened with nonblocking read and no writer exists. What is commonly returned when it is read empty?
options: EOF
A permanently blocking result
A fabricated zero byte
The PID of the next writer
answer: EOF
questions.explanation: With no writer and no buffered data, a FIFO read commonly returns EOF. Nonblocking behavior matters especially while writers exist but no data is available.

questions.prompt: A sender and receiver use a local socket pair created by socketpair. What is a common property?
options: Two connected endpoints are returned directly
A network server must call accept
The endpoints cannot be bidirectional
The endpoints are process IDs
answer: Two connected endpoints are returned directly
questions.explanation: Socketpair creates a pair of connected sockets, often for local interprocess communication without a separate bind/listen/accept sequence.

questions.prompt: A process uses a pipe for two-way communication between parent and child. What is usually needed?
options: Two pipes, one for each direction
One pipe with the same descriptor used for both directions
A condition variable only
A single exit status
answer: Two pipes, one for each direction
questions.explanation: Ordinary pipes are unidirectional byte streams. Two directions are commonly implemented using a pair of pipes, one per direction.

questions.prompt: A message queue is used between processes on one host. How does the receiver commonly obtain message contents?
options: The kernel copies a queued message into its receive buffer
The receiver gets the sender?s stack pointer
The queue remaps the sender?s address space automatically
The kernel changes the sender?s PID
answer: The kernel copies a queued message into its receive buffer
questions.explanation: Kernel-managed message queues usually copy message bytes into the receiver?s supplied buffer, isolating each process?s address space.

questions.prompt: A process writes to shared memory and then exits. What happens to the bytes?
options: They remain in the shared region while that region exists
They are automatically erased at process exit in every case
They are copied into the parent?s stack
They are converted into a message queue
answer: They remain in the shared region while that region exists
questions.explanation: Shared-memory lifetime is governed by the segment/object lifecycle and mappings, not automatically by one process?s exit in every API.

questions.prompt: A producer-consumer buffer has capacity N and uses an empty-slot semaphore initialized to N. What does empty count represent?
options: The number of available buffer slots
The number of consumed items
The number of active processes
The number of bytes in each item
answer: The number of available buffer slots
questions.explanation: The empty semaphore tracks free capacity. A producer waits on it before inserting and signals the full-item count afterward.

questions.prompt: In a bounded buffer, the full-item semaphore is initialized to 0. What does this encode initially?
options: There are no produced items available to consume
The buffer has zero capacity
Every slot is locked by a consumer
The producer has terminated
answer: There are no produced items available to consume
questions.explanation: At startup, the buffer contains no items. A consumer waiting on full blocks until a producer inserts an item and signals.

questions.prompt: A bounded buffer uses a mutex, empty=N, and full=0. Which producer ordering avoids deadlock when the buffer is full?
options: Wait(empty), lock(mutex), insert, unlock, signal(full)
Lock(mutex), wait(empty), insert, signal(full), unlock
Wait(full), insert, signal(empty)
Signal(empty), lock(mutex), wait(full)
answer: Wait(empty), lock(mutex), insert, unlock, signal(full)
questions.explanation: The producer first waits for capacity before taking the mutex. Otherwise it could hold the mutex while waiting for a consumer that needs that mutex to free a slot.

questions.prompt: In a producer-consumer solution, a consumer locks the mutex and then blocks on full while the buffer is empty. What is the bug?
options: It may prevent producers from acquiring the mutex to add data
It frees all empty slots
It makes the pipe bidirectional
It guarantees fairness
answer: It may prevent producers from acquiring the mutex to add data
questions.explanation: The consumer holds the mutex while waiting for an item. A producer then cannot enter the critical section to create that item, causing deadlock.

questions.prompt: A process reads from a pipe after one writer closes its descriptor, while another writer descriptor remains open elsewhere. Does the reader see EOF?
options: No, not until all write descriptors are closed and buffered bytes are drained
Yes, as soon as any writer closes
Yes, regardless of buffered bytes
Only after the reader closes its own end
answer: No, not until all write descriptors are closed and buffered bytes are drained
questions.explanation: EOF requires no remaining write references and no buffered data. Closing one of multiple writer descriptors is insufficient.

questions.prompt: A process inherits a pipe write descriptor across exec because it was not marked close-on-exec. What practical problem can occur?
options: The new program may unintentionally keep the pipe open and delay EOF
The pipe becomes a socket
The parent loses its PID
The descriptor becomes read-only
answer: The new program may unintentionally keep the pipe open and delay EOF
questions.explanation: An inherited write end can keep the pipe?s writer count nonzero. A reader waiting for EOF may therefore block even though the intended writer has finished.

questions.prompt: A socket is in listening state but the server has not called accept. What can happen to incoming connection requests?
options: They may wait in a pending connection queue
They are delivered as shared-memory pages
They execute server code automatically
They change into datagrams
answer: They may wait in a pending connection queue
questions.explanation: The kernel can queue completed or pending connection requests up to configured limits. The server must call accept to obtain a connected socket.

questions.prompt: A client closes its TCP write side but continues reading. What protocol operation does this resemble?
options: Half-close
Process fork
Shared-memory detach
Datagram fragmentation
answer: Half-close
questions.explanation: A TCP half-close signals that the endpoint will send no more bytes while it may continue receiving data from the peer.

questions.prompt: A process sends a signal to another process that is currently blocked in a system call. What may happen?
options: The call may be interrupted or restarted depending on signal and API behavior
The blocked call always completes successfully
The process?s memory becomes shared
The signal becomes a pipe byte
answer: The call may be interrupted or restarted depending on signal and API behavior
questions.explanation: Signal delivery can interrupt certain blocking calls; whether the call returns an interruption error or restarts depends on API flags and signal semantics.

questions.prompt: A sender uses a signal to notify a receiver that shared-memory data is ready. What must the receiver still do?
options: Read and validate the shared data using proper synchronization
Assume the signal carries the entire data payload
Call wait to reap the sender
Create a second shared-memory segment
answer: Read and validate the shared data using proper synchronization
questions.explanation: A signal is only a notification. The receiver must access shared memory and use appropriate synchronization to ensure visibility and consistency.

questions.prompt: A system?s pipe capacity is 4096 bytes. A nonblocking writer attempts to write 6000 bytes while the pipe is empty. What is generally permitted?
options: A partial write or a would-block result, depending on API guarantees
The pipe capacity silently becomes 6000
The write must terminate the process
The data is split into a message queue
answer: A partial write or a would-block result, depending on API guarantees
questions.explanation: Nonblocking writes can complete partially or fail with would-block when the request cannot be accepted atomically. Exact behavior depends on size and system guarantees.

questions.prompt: A message queue contains messages in order A, B, C. A receiver requests the first message of a particular type that is B?s type. What can happen?
options: B can be selected while A remains queued
A must be removed first in all queue APIs
All messages are returned together
The queue is sorted by sender PID
answer: B can be selected while A remains queued
questions.explanation: Typed message queue APIs can select a matching message even if an earlier nonmatching message remains in the queue.

questions.prompt: A shared-memory protocol uses a single Boolean ready flag and allows the producer to overwrite data before the consumer reads it. What failure is possible?
options: The consumer can miss or read overwritten data
The flag becomes a process ID
The mapping automatically locks itself
The consumer receives a duplicate PID
answer: The consumer can miss or read overwritten data
questions.explanation: A Boolean does not count how many items are pending. The producer can overwrite an unread item or collapse multiple events; a queue or sequence/count protocol is needed.

questions.prompt: Two processes map the same shared memory but use different structure layouts due to version mismatch. What is a likely problem?
options: They interpret the same bytes inconsistently
The OS remaps one process to a different PID
The memory becomes a pipe
All reads are automatically byte-swapped
answer: They interpret the same bytes inconsistently
questions.explanation: Shared bytes have no inherent schema. Different offsets, sizes, or versions can cause each process to interpret the same data differently.

questions.prompt: A process wants reliable ordered byte delivery across hosts. Which transport is the usual fit?
options: TCP stream socket
UDP datagram socket
signal
anonymous pipe
answer: TCP stream socket
questions.explanation: TCP provides a reliable ordered byte stream between network endpoints. UDP datagrams do not guarantee delivery or order.

questions.prompt: A process wants message boundaries and tolerates loss or reordering over a network. Which transport may fit?
options: UDP datagram socket
TCP stream socket
anonymous pipe
shared memory
answer: UDP datagram socket
questions.explanation: UDP preserves datagram boundaries at the API but does not guarantee reliable delivery or ordering, matching the stated tolerance.

questions.prompt: A receiver reads a 10-byte pipe write in two calls of 4 and 6 bytes. What does the receiver observe?
options: A 10-byte stream that can be consumed across multiple reads
Two preserved messages of lengths 4 and 6
A single read is guaranteed
The pipe reports EOF after 4 bytes
answer: A 10-byte stream that can be consumed across multiple reads
questions.explanation: Pipes are byte streams. A write boundary does not force the reader to receive that data in one read call.

questions.prompt: A producer has written data into shared memory but crashes before signaling the consumer. What is a concern?
options: The consumer may wait indefinitely despite data being present
The OS signals automatically in every protocol
The shared segment becomes a socket
The consumer sees an exit status as payload
answer: The consumer may wait indefinitely despite data being present
questions.explanation: Data publication and notification are separate steps. If the producer fails between them, the consumer may wait unless the protocol includes recovery or timeouts.

questions.prompt: A pipe contains 120 bytes. A reader consumes 45 bytes. How many bytes remain buffered?
questions.explanation: A pipe is a byte stream. Consuming 45 of 120 leaves 120 ? 45 = 75 bytes.

questions.prompt: A 10,000-byte stream is received in reads of at most 2,500 bytes. Assuming each read returns the maximum available amount, how many reads are needed?
questions.explanation: The bytes are divided into 10,000 / 2,500 = 4 chunks, so four reads retrieve the entire stream.

questions.prompt: A bounded buffer has capacity 12 and currently contains 9 items. How many empty-slot permits should be available?
questions.explanation: Free capacity is total capacity minus occupied slots: 12 ? 9 = 3 permits.

questions.prompt: A bounded buffer has capacity 15 and contains 4 items. What is the full-item semaphore count?
questions.explanation: The full count tracks available items for consumers. There are four buffered items, so the count is four.

questions.prompt: A producer inserts 8 items into an initially empty buffer of capacity 20, with no consumer. How many empty slots remain?
questions.explanation: Eight insertions occupy eight slots. The remaining capacity is 20 ? 8 = 12.

questions.prompt: Three 100-byte messages are sent through a message queue and none is received. How many payload bytes are queued, ignoring metadata?
questions.explanation: The queue retains three discrete messages. Payload storage totals 3 ? 100 = 300 bytes.

questions.prompt: A socket stream contains 8192 bytes. A receiver has already read 3072 bytes. How many bytes remain unread?
questions.explanation: The unread remainder is 8192 ? 3072 = 5120 bytes. Stream sockets preserve the sequence of bytes, not message boundaries.

questions.prompt: A pipe has capacity 4096 bytes and currently holds 1024. How many additional bytes fit before it is full?
questions.explanation: Available pipe capacity is 4096 ? 1024 = 3072 bytes. A larger blocking write may have to wait.

questions.prompt: A shared ring buffer has capacity 16 and currently contains 11 items. How many items can be added without consuming any?
questions.explanation: The ring has 16 total slots and 11 are occupied, leaving 5 free slots.

questions.prompt: A producer signals a semaphore once for each of 23 inserted items. The consumer has completed 17 waits. How many item permits remain, assuming no other operations?
questions.explanation: Each signal adds one permit and each successful wait consumes one. The remaining count is 23 ? 17 = 6.

questions.prompt: Two unidirectional pipes are used to create a parent-child request/response channel. How many pipe endpoints exist in total?
questions.explanation: Each pipe has a read endpoint and a write endpoint. Two pipes therefore have 2 ? 2 = 4 endpoints.

questions.prompt: A stream protocol sends a 4-byte length header followed by a 120-byte payload per frame. What is the total frame size in bytes?
questions.explanation: The frame consists of a 4-byte header and 120 payload bytes, giving 124 bytes total.

questions.prompt: A FIFO has 500 buffered bytes. The only writer closes, and the reader consumes 200 bytes. How many bytes remain before EOF is returned?
questions.explanation: Closing the final writer does not discard buffered data. After consuming 200 of 500 bytes, 300 remain; EOF follows once drained.

questions.prompt: A semaphore has count 9. Five successful waits and two signals occur. What is the final count?
questions.explanation: Each wait subtracts one and each signal adds one: 9 ? 5 + 2 = 6.

questions.prompt: A ring buffer capacity is 10. A consumer removes 3 items and a producer adds 6, starting from 4 items. How many items are present at the end?
questions.explanation: The occupancy is 4 ? 3 + 6 = 7, which is within the capacity of 10.

questions.prompt: Which are properties of ordinary anonymous pipes?
options: They provide byte-stream communication
They are commonly accessed through file descriptors
They preserve application message boundaries automatically
They can connect parent and child after descriptor inheritance
answer: They provide byte-stream communication
They are commonly accessed through file descriptors
They can connect parent and child after descriptor inheritance
questions.explanation: Pipes are descriptor-based byte streams and are often inherited across fork. They do not inherently preserve application message boundaries.

questions.prompt: Which actions are important when setting up a one-way pipe between parent and child?
options: Close unused read or write ends in each process
Connect producer output to the write end
Connect consumer input to the read end
Keep every descriptor open so EOF arrives sooner
answer: Close unused read or write ends in each process
Connect producer output to the write end
Connect consumer input to the read end
questions.explanation: Closing unused ends prevents accidental blocking and enables correct EOF detection. The producer writes and consumer reads; extra open descriptors delay EOF.

questions.prompt: Which statements about shared memory are correct?
options: It allows direct access to common mapped bytes
It requires synchronization for concurrent conflicting accesses
Processes may map it at different virtual addresses
It automatically defines message boundaries
answer: It allows direct access to common mapped bytes
It requires synchronization for concurrent conflicting accesses
Processes may map it at different virtual addresses
questions.explanation: Shared memory exposes common bytes and mappings can differ in virtual address. The application defines structure and synchronization; boundaries are not automatic.

questions.prompt: Which are valid IPC mechanisms between unrelated local processes?
options: Named FIFO
Message queue
Unix-domain socket
An anonymous pipe with no inherited descriptor and no transfer mechanism
answer: Named FIFO
Message queue
Unix-domain socket
questions.explanation: Named FIFOs, kernel message queues, and Unix-domain sockets can establish communication between unrelated processes. An unreachable anonymous pipe cannot.

questions.prompt: Which are appropriate ways to frame messages over a TCP byte stream?
options: Length prefix
Delimiter with escaping rules
Fixed-size records
Assume one receive call returns one send call
answer: Length prefix
Delimiter with escaping rules
Fixed-size records
questions.explanation: Length fields, delimiters, or fixed record sizes can define application framing. TCP does not preserve send/receive call boundaries.

questions.prompt: Which properties are generally associated with UDP datagrams?
options: Message boundaries are preserved at the API
Delivery is not guaranteed
Ordering is not guaranteed
A receiver always obtains every datagram exactly once
answer: Message boundaries are preserved at the API
Delivery is not guaranteed
Ordering is not guaranteed
questions.explanation: UDP delivers message-oriented datagrams but offers no general delivery, ordering, or exactly-once guarantee.

questions.prompt: Which statements about message queues are correct?
options: They store discrete messages
They can decouple sender and receiver timing
A bounded queue can block or reject a send when full
They require sender and receiver to access one shared pointer
answer: They store discrete messages
They can decouple sender and receiver timing
A bounded queue can block or reject a send when full
questions.explanation: Queues retain messages in kernel-managed storage and allow asynchronous communication. Capacity limits can cause blocking or errors; direct shared pointers are not required.

questions.prompt: Which statements about signals are correct?
options: They are useful for asynchronous event notification
They are generally poor channels for large payloads
A blocked signal may remain pending
They provide a reliable ordered byte stream
answer: They are useful for asynchronous event notification
They are generally poor channels for large payloads
A blocked signal may remain pending
questions.explanation: Signals notify events and can remain pending while blocked, but they do not provide arbitrary bulk transfer or stream ordering.

questions.prompt: Which steps support a correct bounded-buffer producer protocol?
options: Wait for an empty slot
Acquire the buffer mutex before modifying indices
Release the mutex after insertion
Signal that an item is available after insertion
answer: Wait for an empty slot
Acquire the buffer mutex before modifying indices
Release the mutex after insertion
Signal that an item is available after insertion
questions.explanation: The producer must reserve capacity, modify buffer state under mutual exclusion, then publish item availability. This prevents overflow and races.

questions.prompt: Which steps support a correct bounded-buffer consumer protocol?
options: Wait for an available item
Acquire the mutex before removing it
Release the mutex after updating indices
Signal an empty slot after removal
answer: Wait for an available item
Acquire the mutex before removing it
Release the mutex after updating indices
Signal an empty slot after removal
questions.explanation: The consumer waits for data, safely removes it under the mutex, and signals newly available capacity so producers can continue.

questions.prompt: Which issues can arise from failing to close unused pipe descriptors?
options: A reader may not observe EOF
A writer may not receive broken-pipe notification
The descriptor can keep a pipe endpoint logically open
The pipe automatically becomes bidirectional
answer: A reader may not observe EOF
A writer may not receive broken-pipe notification
The descriptor can keep a pipe endpoint logically open
questions.explanation: Open references affect EOF and broken-pipe conditions. Keeping unused endpoints open can suppress those conditions; it does not change pipe directionality.

questions.prompt: Which statements about socket communication are correct?
options: A stream socket may require application framing
A listening socket and accepted connection socket serve different roles
Unix-domain sockets can communicate locally
Every socket protocol guarantees reliable delivery
answer: A stream socket may require application framing
A listening socket and accepted connection socket serve different roles
Unix-domain sockets can communicate locally
questions.explanation: Stream sockets need framing, and servers use a listening endpoint plus connected endpoints. Local sockets are supported; reliability depends on the protocol.

questions.prompt: Which statements about shared-memory pointers are correct?
options: A raw pointer may be invalid in another process
Offsets from the segment base can support relocatable structures
The same physical pages can map at different virtual addresses
A pointer value is automatically translated between processes
answer: A raw pointer may be invalid in another process
Offsets from the segment base can support relocatable structures
The same physical pages can map at different virtual addresses
questions.explanation: Virtual pointers are process-relative. Storing offsets allows relocation, and shared physical pages can be mapped differently; raw pointer translation is not automatic.

questions.prompt: Which can help recover from a producer crash during shared-memory IPC?
options: A robust process-shared mutex
A generation counter or sequence number
Timeout and liveness checks
Assuming every notification is delivered exactly once
answer: A robust process-shared mutex
A generation counter or sequence number
Timeout and liveness checks
questions.explanation: Robust locks, explicit protocol state, and liveness detection help identify and recover from partial updates. Assuming perfect notification is unsafe.

questions.prompt: Which statements distinguish a semaphore from a condition variable?
options: A semaphore maintains a permit count
A condition-variable signal is not usually retained for future waiters
A semaphore wait can consume a permit signaled earlier
Both must always be used without a mutex
answer: A semaphore maintains a permit count
A condition-variable signal is not usually retained for future waiters
A semaphore wait can consume a permit signaled earlier
questions.explanation: Semaphores retain counts; condition notifications do not generally persist. Condition variables are typically paired with a mutex and predicate.

questions.prompt: Which choices are suitable for bidirectional local IPC?
options: A Unix-domain stream socket
A socket pair
Two ordinary pipes
A single ordinary unidirectional pipe used only in its supported direction
answer: A Unix-domain stream socket
A socket pair
Two ordinary pipes
questions.explanation: Unix-domain sockets, socket pairs, or two pipes can carry data in both directions. One ordinary pipe has one data direction.

questions.prompt: Which statements about pipe atomicity are correct?
options: Small writes up to PIPE_BUF are commonly protected from interleaving
Atomicity does not guarantee which writer goes first
A large write is always one indivisible message
Pipe reads preserve each write boundary
answer: Small writes up to PIPE_BUF are commonly protected from interleaving
Atomicity does not guarantee which writer goes first
questions.explanation: The PIPE_BUF guarantee concerns interleaving of suitably small writes, not scheduling order. Larger writes and read boundaries do not become atomic messages.

questions.prompt: Which IPC mechanisms can preserve discrete records without application framing over a byte stream?
options: Message queues
Datagram sockets
Pipes
TCP stream sockets
answer: Message queues
Datagram sockets
questions.explanation: Message queues and datagram sockets preserve message units. Pipes and TCP expose streams, so applications must define framing.

questions.prompt: Which are consequences of a shared-memory design?
options: Low overhead for repeated large data exchange
Application must design synchronization
Processes must agree on a data layout
Kernel copies each field on every access
answer: Low overhead for repeated large data exchange
Application must design synchronization
Processes must agree on a data layout
questions.explanation: Shared mappings can reduce copying, but correctness depends on synchronization and a compatible data layout. Loads/stores access mapped pages directly.

questions.prompt: Which events can wake a process blocked in IPC?
options: Data arrives on an empty pipe
A message matching its queue receive arrives
A semaphore permit becomes available
A process changes its current working directory
answer: Data arrives on an empty pipe
A message matching its queue receive arrives
A semaphore permit becomes available
questions.explanation: IPC waits become ready when their awaited resource or event occurs. An unrelated working-directory change does not satisfy these waits.

questions.prompt: A receiver needs to distinguish an empty pipe from a temporarily empty but still open pipe. Which condition distinguishes EOF?
options: No data remains and every write descriptor is closed
No data is currently buffered
The writer has not yet called write
The reader has a nonblocking flag
answer: No data remains and every write descriptor is closed
questions.explanation: An empty pipe can still receive future bytes while any write end remains open. EOF requires both an empty buffer and no remaining writers.

questions.prompt: A process sends a 50 KiB structure through a pipe and the receiver reads 8 KiB at a time. What should the receiver do to reconstruct it?
options: Accumulate bytes until the protocol-defined length is reached
Assume the first read contains the whole structure
Treat each read as a separate record
Use the sender PID as a delimiter
answer: Accumulate bytes until the protocol-defined length is reached
questions.explanation: Pipes are streams, so one logical object can span multiple reads. The receiver must use framing, such as a known length, to reconstruct it.

questions.prompt: Two process-shared mutexes protect the same data but are acquired in inconsistent order by two processes. What risk remains?
options: Deadlock from circular lock ordering
Automatic deadlock prevention by shared memory
Message loss due to TCP
The data becomes immutable
answer: Deadlock from circular lock ordering
questions.explanation: If one process holds mutex A while waiting for B and another holds B while waiting for A, neither can proceed. Shared memory does not prevent this cycle.

questions.prompt: A TCP client calls send repeatedly until all bytes are accepted. Why may this loop be necessary?
options: A send call can accept fewer bytes than requested
TCP preserves message boundaries and splits by call
The kernel rejects every second send
The peer must issue one receive per send
answer: A send call can accept fewer bytes than requested
questions.explanation: Stream send calls may be partial, so robust code advances through the unsent suffix until the full buffer is accepted or an error occurs.

questions.prompt: A datagram receiver gets a zero-length UDP datagram. What does that mean?
options: A valid datagram with an empty payload may have arrived
The peer necessarily closed the connection
The socket is always at EOF
A process became a zombie
answer: A valid datagram with an empty payload may have arrived
questions.explanation: UDP is message-oriented and can carry a datagram with zero payload bytes. This differs from stream EOF semantics.
